title: The More You See It, the More You Like It
text:
In 1968 the psychologist Robert Zajonc of the University of Michigan published a set of experiments on a simple question: does merely seeing something again and again make us like it more?

In one study he showed people made-up words presented as Turkish, such as "iktitaf" and "civadra." Some words appeared once, others two, five, ten or twenty-five times, in random order. Afterward participants guessed whether each word meant something good or bad. The more often they had seen a word, the more likely they were to guess it had a pleasant meaning. He found the same pattern with Chinese-looking characters and with photographs of unfamiliar faces from a college yearbook: faces shown more often were rated as more likable.

Nothing about the words or faces had changed, and participants learned nothing new about them. Only familiarity had grown. Zajonc called this the mere exposure effect. Later research found it works even when images are flashed too briefly to be consciously seen, though it can weaken or reverse with overexposure or when first reactions are negative.
lesson: Familiarity breeds liking more often than contempt. Showing up regularly, in person and in small ways, warms people to you before any word is said.
location: University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA
source: Zajonc, R. B. (1968). Attitudinal effects of mere exposure. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology Monograph Supplement, 9(2, Part 2), 1-27.
